title: Homework 01
text:
TidyTuesday Part
Explore the week’s TidyTuesday challenge. Develop a research question, then answer it through a short data story mainly composed of effective visualizations. Provide sufficient background for readers to grasp your narrative. Refer to the Homework Instructions ⭐ page on the course website for details on how to submit this part.
Codecappuccino_index <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-09-08/cappuccino_index.csv')
Codelibrary(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
Codeggplot(cappuccino_index, aes(x = index)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 5,
    fill = "lightblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Countries by Cappuccino Index Range",
    subtitle= "The Cost for Countries in Reality",
    x = "Cappuccino Index (in minutes)",
    y = "Number of Countries",
    caption = "Alara Yener, 9/16/2026, cappuccino_index.csv",
    alt = "This is a historgram that shows the cappuccino index in minutes on the x-axis and the number of countries on the y-axis. There is a strong left skew, however there is an outlier on the far right."
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16))
Codeextremes <- cappuccino_index |>
  slice_max(index, n = 10) |>
  bind_rows(slice_min(cappuccino_index, index, n = 10)) |>
  distinct(country, .keep_all = TRUE)
Codeggplot(extremes, aes(
  x = reorder(country, index),
  y = index
)) +
  geom_col(fill = "lightblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Seeing Price Inequalities Through Coffee",
    subtitle= "The 20 Most Extreme Cases",
    caption = "By: Alara Yener, Created on: 9/16/2026, Sourced from: cappuccino_index.csv",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Minutes of work needed to purchase a small cup of coffee",
    alt = "Horizontal bar chart showing the 20 countries with the highest and lowest minutes needed to be worked to get a cappuccino. The x-axis has the number of minutes of work needed to purchase a cappuccino and the y-axis lists those most extreme 20 countries. "
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16)) +
  theme_classic()
How Much Work Does a Cappuccino Actually Cost?
A cappuccino is more than just the price listed on a menu. Its affordability can vary depending on how much a worker earns. The Cappuccino Index measures affordability by estimating the number of minutes a barista must work to afford a small cappuccino in their country. My research question is:
How does the amount of time workers need to work to afford a cappuccino vary across countries?
From this research question I looked at the overall distribution of countries in relation to the number of minutes they would have to work. After this inital exploration, I was curious about the extremes. This prompted me to take a look at the 10 countries that take the least amount of time to purchase a cappuccino and the ten countries where is takes the most amount of time. This goes to show how much a cappuccino can cost strikingly different amounts depending on what country you are in.

title: Homework 02
text:
TidyTuesday Part (Optional)
Explore the week’s TidyTuesday challenge. Develop a research question, then answer it through a short data story mainly composed of effective visualizations. Provide sufficient background for readers to grasp your narrative. Refer to the Homework Instructions ⭐ page on the course website for details on how to submit this part.
Codelibrary(ggplot2)
dead_sea_scrolls <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-09-15/dead_sea_scrolls.csv')
Codeggplot(dead_sea_scrolls,aes(x = period, fill = material)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = "Dead Sea Scrolls by Period and Material",
    subtitle= "Parchment dominates across the board, with the Herodian period having the most manuscripts",
    caption = "By: Alara Yener, Created on: 9/22/2026, Sourced from: Dead Sea Scrolls Manuscripts",
    x = "Period",
    y = "Number of Manuscripts",
    fill = "Material",
    alt = "Bar chart displaying time period on the x-axis and the number of manuscripts on the y access. With each bar being color coded on which material each manuscrip is made out of."
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 6),
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.margin = margin(t=50)
  )
How does the material of Dead Sea Scroll manuscripts vary across different historical periods?
The Dead Sea Scrolls provide an important look into the manuscripts and written materials preserved from the ancient world. This visualization examines the relationship between the historical period of a manuscript and the material it was written on. The data shows that parchment is the most prominent material across the periods represented in the dataset, while the Herodian period has the largest number of manuscripts. These patterns suggest that parchment was widely represented among the surviving manuscripts, particularly among those dated to the Herodian period. The visualization gives us a way to compare how manuscript materials are seen from across the different periods in the dataset.

title: HW02-P1 Adv Data Viz
text:
Visualization

Code# Code for recreating the visualization
# Use as many code chunks as you need to organize your work well



Codemonth_start <- weather %>%
  group_by(Month) %>%
  summarize(
    dateInYear = min(dateInYear))

month_labels <- weather %>%
  group_by(Month) %>%
  summarize(
    dateInYear = mean(dateInYear))

weather_temp_plot <- ggplot(weather) +
    geom_linerange(
    aes(
      x = dateInYear,
      ymin = RecordLow,
      ymax = RecordHigh),
    color = "#ECEBE3") +
  
  geom_linerange(
    aes(
      x = dateInYear,
      ymin = NormalLow,
      ymax = NormalHigh),
    color = "#C8B8BA") +
  
  geom_linerange(
    aes(
      x = dateInYear,
      ymin = Low,
      ymax = High),
    color = "#A90248") +
  
  geom_vline(
    data = month_start,
    aes(xintercept = dateInYear),
    color = "white") +
  
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = month_labels$dateInYear,
    labels = month.abb) +
  theme_classic()
